On the Pleasure of Getting Lost  

One of the quiet luxuries of the modern world—though it can look, at first glance, like an inconvenience—is the capacity to become lost on purpose. A map is nearly always waiting in your pocket: open the phone, tap the blue dot, and the disorientation collapses. Yet because the solution is so close at hand, choosing not to reach for it becomes an oddly defiant, revitalizing act.

When I step off a train in a city I’ve never visited, I like to turn the data connection off. The screen goes blank, the battery sighs, and suddenly the pavement feels physical again. The first thing that returns is the scent of the place—diesel, sea salt, coriander from a vendor’s cart—fragrances that never quite survive the journey through fiber-optic cables. Overhead, unfamiliar birds annotate the sky with shapes and sounds you have no names for. You take a left because the cobblestones angle that way, a right because a warped façade in robin-egg blue invites your curiosity, and a detour to follow the echo of music filtering through a half-open window. Your pace falls into the tempo of whatever you’re absorbing, rather than the algorithmic urgency of a route planner.

Entire micro-worlds bloom in front of you once you accept not knowing exactly where you are. In Ljubljana, I stumbled onto a secondhand bookshop hidden in what looked like an old carriage house. Inside, a gray-haired owner fussed with a manual typewriter, producing insertion cards for the shelves; he slid me a volume of locally printed poetry and insisted I keep it if I could pronounce even half the Slovene words. (Reader, I failed. He gave me the book anyway.) In Kyoto, turning down a dead-end alley unveiled a tiny, unattended shrine, no taller than my hip, its stone foxes garlanded with paper cranes. On a misty afternoon in Bogotá, losing the rhythm of the numbered calles brought me to a café where the barista described each coffee bean the way an astronomer names distant stars.

These moments thrive on the negative space of a plan, the deliberate embrace of ambiguity. There’s a cognitive switch that flips when we move from plotting to roaming: the brain’s default-mode network perks up, the unfocused introspective circuitry that fuses memory, imagination, and self-reflection. Paradoxically, it’s when we have no fixed destination that we begin to notice how everything interconnects. A patch of graffiti echoes a line from a childhood song; the cadence of strangers’ footsteps merges with an old conversation in your memory; you remember, for reasons unclear, the first time you laughed so hard your ribs hurt. Your senses vote to stay awake.

This is not nostalgia for a bygone era when getting lost was mandatory. The contemporary toolkit is miraculous, and sometimes life depends on it. But the fact that we no longer have to be lost makes the experience elective, almost artistic. Like fasting in a time of abundance, or writing by hand when keyboards dominate, voluntary disorientation sharpens faculties dulled by optimization.

The practice scales beyond travel. Read a novel in a genre you secretly dismiss. Listen to a playlist assembled by someone whose taste baffles you. Browse a grocery aisle where the labels are in a language you don’t speak, and try constructing dinner from puzzles of unknown flavor. The goal isn’t novelty for novelty’s sake, but to widen the margins of perception—to court the serendipity that slips in when certainty steps out.

Eventually, of course, you will rejoin the grid. Screens will light, schedules resume, and the algorithm will shepherd you back to whichever rectangle of routine you inhabit. But you’ll bring with you a small cache of images that nobody else could have scrolled to find: the sound of rain ricocheting off terracotta roofs, the way a stranger’s laugh in a night market carried your name even though it wasn’t calling you, the mysterious confidence that the world is larger than the routes that lead directly through it.

In a culture devoted to efficiency, getting lost is a slow, stubborn form of wisdom—a reminder that meaning often waits off-map, around the corner we almost didn’t take.
